theme: Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD?
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 24. Yesterday’s psalm asked who may stand in God’s presence. Today’s asks the same question again, and then celebrates the arrival of the King. Read the last section, verses 7 to 10, aloud as a procession.
settingTheScene: Psalm 24 is a psalm of David and was probably sung when the ark was brought up to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6). It has three parts: the earth belongs to the LORD (vv. 1-2), only the pure may come into his presence (vv. 3-6), and the gates must open for the King of glory (vv. 7-10). It joins together the tabernacle themes you have been reading about this week: God’s holiness, the need for clean hands, and the ark of his presence.
observation: “The earth is the LORD’s and the fullness thereof, the world and those who dwell in it” (v. 1).
He “has founded it upon the seas and established it upon the rivers” (v. 2).
“Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? And who shall stand in his holy place?” (v. 3).
“He who has clean hands and a pure heart, who does not lift up his soul to what is false and does not swear deceitfully” (v. 4).
“He will receive blessing from the LORD and righteousness from the God of his salvation” (v. 5).
“Lift up your heads, O gates! And be lifted up, O ancient doors, that the King of glory may come in” (v. 7).
“Who is this King of glory? The LORD, strong and mighty, the LORD, mighty in battle!” (v. 8).
The question is asked again, and the answer changes: “The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory!” (v. 10).
interpretation:
The psalm opens with a broad claim: everything belongs to God. He founded the earth. It is not a neutral world that we are free to use as we like. The earth is his. That is the basis for all that follows. The God who owns the world has the right to say who may come to his house.

Then comes the question of verse 3, the same as Psalm 15. The answer is about hands and heart: outward and inward cleanness. Notice that the one who ascends “will receive blessing from the LORD and righteousness from the God of his salvation.” Righteousness here is something received. It is not only earned. The one who is fit to stand in God’s presence has been given a righteousness he did not make.

The last section is a drama. The procession arrives at the gates of Jerusalem with the ark, and the gates are told to open. A voice from inside asks, “Who is this King of glory?” The answer comes: the LORD, strong and mighty in battle. The same exchange is repeated, and the title grows: “the LORD of hosts.” The ark is the sign of God’s presence, and the God who comes is a conquering King.

Look at how the psalm moves. It begins with the earth belonging to God, then asks who can come near to him, and ends with the King coming to us. The answer to the problem of who may ascend the hill is that the King descends. He comes to the gates, and he asks to be let in. It is a picture of the God who draws near to his people.
connection: The early church read this psalm as a picture of Christ’s ascension. He is the one with clean hands and a pure heart, who ascended the holy hill and now sits at the right hand of the Father (Ephesians 4:8-10; Hebrews 4:14). Paul says that “the earth is the Lord’s, and everything in it” (1 Corinthians 10:26). Revelation 19:11-16 shows the King of glory returning as a conqueror. Jesus also stands at the door of the church and knocks (Revelation 3:20).
application:
Think of one thing in your life you tend to treat as belonging to you: money, time, or plans. Say aloud, “This is the LORD’s.”

Pray verse 7 as an invitation. Ask the King of glory to come in to a part of your life you have kept closed.

Thank Jesus that he ascended on your behalf, and that you can follow him.
prayerPrompts: Welcome the King of glory into the rooms of your life that you tend to keep closed.
Thank Jesus for ascending with clean hands and a pure heart.
Praise him as the owner of everything.
